lessons.title: Brood stock and spawning
lessons.html:
Where baby fish come from

Every fish farm needs young fish to grow. They come from a hatchery, which can be on the farm or a separate business. The hatchery keeps adult breeding fish called brood stock.

Looking after brood stock

  • Choose healthy, fast-growing fish with good shape and no defects.
  • Keep males and females apart until breeding time on many farms.
  • Feed them good quality brood stock feed.
  • Keep water quality and temperature right for the species.
  • Handle them gently and as little as possible. Stress can stop them breeding.
  • Mark or tag them and keep records of each fish's breeding.

How different species breed

SpeciesHow breeding works
TilapiaBreeds easily in ponds and tanks. The female keeps the eggs and young fry in her mouth to protect them (mouth brooding).
CatfishUsually needs help in the hatchery. Trained staff may use a hormone treatment and then strip eggs and milt by hand.
TroutBreeds once a year in winter. Eggs and milt are stripped by hand from ripe fish.
AbaloneRipe adults are made to spawn in tanks; eggs and sperm are mixed in the water.

Stripping and fertilising

Stripping means gently pressing the belly of a ripe fish to squeeze out eggs (female) or milt (male). The eggs and milt are mixed so the eggs are fertilised. Only trained staff should strip fish, because rough pressing can injure them. Hormones and anaesthetics may only be used by trained staff following the label and the vet's advice.

lessons.title: Eggs, larvae and fry
lessons.html:
Caring for eggs

Fertilised eggs are kept in incubators, such as trays or jars with clean water flowing through them.

  • Keep the water clean, with plenty of oxygen and at the right temperature for the species.
  • Keep eggs out of strong light.
  • Remove dead eggs every day. Dead eggs turn white and grow fungus, which spreads to live eggs. Use a clean pipette or soft tweezers.
  • Do not knock or shake the incubators.

Larvae

When the egg hatches, a tiny larva comes out with a yolk sac on its belly. The yolk sac is its food for the first days. The larva does not need to be fed until the yolk sac is almost used up.

First feeding

When the yolk sac is nearly gone, the larvae start to swim up and look for food. This is a critical time. If they do not get the right food at the right time, many will die.

  • Feed very small amounts, many times a day.
  • Use the special starter feed (fine powder or crumbs), or live food such as tiny water animals, as the hatchery manager says.
  • Watch that the fry are eating. Their bellies should look full.
  • Clean tanks gently to remove leftover feed and waste.

Fry

As fry grow, they get bigger feed, in the size shown on the feeding chart. Feed size must fit the fish's mouth. Too big and they cannot eat it; too small and it is wasted.

Common problems

  • Poor water quality from overfeeding.
  • Fungus on eggs.
  • Bigger fry eating smaller ones (especially catfish). Sort fry by size.
  • Disease spreading quickly in crowded tanks.

lessons.title: Rearing fingerlings and hatchery hygiene
lessons.html:
From fry to fingerling

When fry reach about the size of a finger they are called fingerlings. They are moved to bigger tanks or nursery ponds, or sold to grow-out farms.

Grading

Fish of the same age grow at different speeds. Grading means sorting them by size using graders (boxes with bars or mesh that let small fish through). Grading:

  • Stops big fish eating or bullying small ones.
  • Lets every fish get feed.
  • Makes feeding and counting easier.

Grade gently, in water if possible, and in the cool part of the day. Stop feeding for some hours before grading, as your supervisor instructs.

Counting and stocking

Count fingerlings by weighing a sample, counting it and working out the total. Do not put too many fish in one tank. The stocking density on the farm plan tells you how many.

Moving fish

  • Move fish in water with enough oxygen.
  • Match the water temperature before releasing them into the new tank.
  • Keep the trip short and the fish shaded.

Hatchery hygiene

Young fish get sick easily. Diseases spread fast in a hatchery.

  • Wash hands and use the foot bath at the hatchery door.
  • Use separate nets and buckets for each tank, or disinfect them between tanks.
  • Do not let visitors walk in without permission.
  • Remove dead fish and eggs every day and record numbers.
  • Keep new fish from other farms apart until the manager says they can join.

Key points

  • Brood stock must be healthy, well fed and handled gently.
  • Only trained staff may strip fish or use hormones and anaesthetics.
  • Remove dead eggs daily so fungus does not spread.
  • First feeding is critical: small amounts, many times a day.
  • Grade fish by size and keep strict hatchery hygiene.
